Nighthawks. Edward Hopper's 1942 painting is his quintessential American work, depicting a handful of solitary figures in a late-night diner bathed in fluorescent light, surrounded by empty streets. It captures urban isolation and melancholy with spare realism, becoming an iconic meditation on loneliness within the modern city.

Painted during World War II, Nighthawks is now at the Art Institute of Chicago and is widely considered Hopper's masterpiece and one of the most recognizable American paintings. The scene shows three patrons—a couple and a lone man—and a server in a corner diner lit by bright interior light, while the street outside is dark and deserted. The composition uses sharp geometric forms, the triangular diner window, harsh shadows, and rectangular street shapes to emphasize isolation and the barrier between interior and exterior worlds.

Hopper's figures are introspective and disconnected from one another despite occupying the same space, a visual metaphor for emotional isolation even among people. The painting is carefully composed to exclude any sign of life outside the diner, heightening the sense of a sealed-off microcosm. It has become a cultural touchstone for American melancholy and urban alienation, referenced endlessly in literature, film, and popular imagination.
